By completing the final column in the truth table below, we obtain the following:

| $\,X\,$ | $\,Y\,$ | $\,¬(X⇔Y)\,$ | $\,(X∧¬Y)∨(¬X∧Y)\,$ | $\,¬(X⇔Y)⇒[(X∧¬Y)∨(¬X∧Y)]\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |

questions.worked_solution:
An expression is a tautology if it is always true, regardless of the inputs.

By completing the final column in the truth table below, we obtain the following:

| $\,X\,$ | $\,Y\,$ | $\,X∧¬Y\,$ | $\,X⇒Y\,$ | $\,(X∧¬Y)∨(X⇒Y)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |

According to the table, $(X∧¬Y)∨(X⇒Y)$ 
$\text{is}$
always true. Therefore, it 
$\text{is}$
a tautology.

questions.worked_solution:
An expression is a tautology if it is always true, regardless of the inputs.

By completing the final column in the truth table below, we obtain the following:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,¬A⇒¬B\,$ | $\,B⇒A\,$ | $\,(¬A⇒¬B)⇒(B⇒A)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |

According to the table, $(¬A⇒¬B)⇒(B⇒A)$ 
$\text{is}$
always true. Therefore, it 
$\text{is}$
a tautology.

An expression is a tautology if it is always true, regardless of the inputs.

By completing the final column in the truth table below, we obtain the following:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,A∨¬B\,$ | $\,B⇒A\,$ | $\,(A∨¬B)⇒(B⇒A)\,$ |

| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |

questions.worked_solution:
An expression is a tautology if it is always true, regardless of the inputs.

By completing the final column in the truth table below, we obtain the following:

| $\,X\,$ | $\,Y\,$ | $\,¬X∧Y\,$ | $\,(¬X⇒Y)⇒X\,$ | $\,(¬X∧Y)∨[(¬X⇒Y)⇒X]\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |

According to the table, $(¬X∧Y)∨[(¬X⇒Y)⇒X]$ 
$\text{is}$
always true. Therefore, it 
$\text{is}$
a tautology.

An expression is a contradiction if it is always false, regardless of the inputs.

By completing the final column in the truth table below, we obtain the following:

| $\,X\,$ | $\,Y\,$ | $\,X∨¬X\,$ | $\,X∧Y\,$ | $\,(X∨¬X)⇒(X∧Y)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |

According to the table, $(X∨¬X)⇒(X∧Y)$

questions.problem:
If $P$ is a statement, $\text{t}$ is a tautology, and $\text{c}$ is a contradiction, complete the following table of logical equivalences.

| Statement | Is Logically Equivalent To |
| --- | --- |
| $\text{c}∧\text{t}$ | {{field-1}} |
| $\text{c}∨\text{t}$ | {{field-2}} |
| $\text{t}∧¬P$ | {{field-3}} |
| $\text{t}∨P$ | {{field-4}} |
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following properties of tautologies and contradictions:

$$
\begin{aligned}A∨\text{t}=\text{t}\, &  & A∧\text{t} & =A \\ A∨\text{c}=A\, &  & A∧\text{c} & =\text{c} \\ \text{t}∨\text{t}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{t}∧\text{t} & =\text{t} \\ \text{t}∨\text{c}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{t}∧\text{c} & =\text{c} \\ \text{c}∨\text{t}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{c}∧\text{t} & =\text{c} \\ \text{c}∨\text{c}=\text{c}\, &  & \text{c}∧\text{c} & =\text{c}\end{aligned}
$$

The completed table is shown below.

| Statement | Is Logically Equivalent To |
| --- | --- |
| $\text{c}∧\text{t}$ | $\text{c}$ |
| $\text{c}∨\text{t}$ | $\text{t}$ |
| $\text{t}∧¬P$ | $¬P$ |
| $\text{t}∨P$ | $\text{t}$ |

questions.problem:
If $P$ is a statement, $\text{t}$ is a tautology, and $\text{c}$ is a contradiction, complete the following table of logical equivalences.

| Statement | Is Logically Equivalent To |
| --- | --- |
| $\text{t}∧\text{t}$ | {{field-1}} |
| $\text{c}∧\text{c}$ | {{field-2}} |
| $\text{c}∨P$ | {{field-3}} |
| $\text{t}∧P$ | {{field-4}} |
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following properties of tautologies and contradictions:

$$
\begin{aligned}A∨\text{t}=\text{t}\, &  & A∧\text{t} & =A \\ A∨\text{c}=A\, &  & A∧\text{c} & =\text{c} \\ \text{t}∨\text{t}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{t}∧\text{t} & =\text{t} \\ \text{t}∨\text{c}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{t}∧\text{c} & =\text{c} \\ \text{c}∨\text{t}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{c}∧\text{t} & =\text{c} \\ \text{c}∨\text{c}=\text{c}\, &  & \text{c}∧\text{c} & =\text{c}\end{aligned}
$$

The completed table is shown below.

| Statement | Is Logically Equivalent To |
| --- | --- |
| $\text{t}∧\text{t}$ | $\text{t}$ |
| $\text{c}∧\text{c}$ | $\text{c}$ |
| $\text{c}∨P$ | $P$ |
| $\text{t}∧P$ | $P$ |

questions.problem:
If $P$ is a statement, $\text{t}$ is a tautology, and $\text{c}$ is a contradiction, complete the following table of logical equivalences.

| Statement | Is Logically Equivalent To |
| --- | --- |
| $\text{t}∧\text{t}$ | {{field-1}} |
| $\text{t}∨\text{c}$ | {{field-2}} |
| $\text{c}∨¬P$ | {{field-3}} |
| $\text{t}∨P$ | {{field-4}} |
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following properties of tautologies and contradictions:

$$
\begin{aligned}A∨\text{t}=\text{t}\, &  & A∧\text{t} & =A \\ A∨\text{c}=A\, &  & A∧\text{c} & =\text{c} \\ \text{t}∨\text{t}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{t}∧\text{t} & =\text{t} \\ \text{t}∨\text{c}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{t}∧\text{c} & =\text{c} \\ \text{c}∨\text{t}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{c}∧\text{t} & =\text{c} \\ \text{c}∨\text{c}=\text{c}\, &  & \text{c}∧\text{c} & =\text{c}\end{aligned}
$$

The completed table is shown below.

| Statement | Is Logically Equivalent To |
| --- | --- |
| $\text{t}∧\text{t}$ | $\text{t}$ |
| $\text{t}∨\text{c}$ | $\text{t}$ |
| $\text{c}∨¬P$ | $¬P$ |
| $\text{t}∨P$ | $\text{t}$ |

questions.problem:
If $P$ is a statement, $\text{t}$ is a tautology, and $\text{c}$ is a contradiction, complete the following table of logical equivalences.

| Statement | Is Logically Equivalent To |
| --- | --- |
| $\text{c}∧\text{c}$ | {{field-1}} |
| $\text{c}∨\text{t}$ | {{field-2}} |
| $P∧\text{c}$ | {{field-3}} |
| $\text{c}∨¬P$ | {{field-4}} |
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following properties of tautologies and contradictions:

$$
\begin{aligned}A∨\text{t}=\text{t}\, &  & A∧\text{t} & =A \\ A∨\text{c}=A\, &  & A∧\text{c} & =\text{c} \\ \text{t}∨\text{t}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{t}∧\text{t} & =\text{t} \\ \text{t}∨\text{c}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{t}∧\text{c} & =\text{c} \\ \text{c}∨\text{t}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{c}∧\text{t} & =\text{c} \\ \text{c}∨\text{c}=\text{c}\, &  & \text{c}∧\text{c} & =\text{c}\end{aligned}
$$

The completed table is shown below.

| Statement | Is Logically Equivalent To |
| --- | --- |
| $\text{c}∧\text{c}$ | $\text{c}$ |
| $\text{c}∨\text{t}$ | $\text{t}$ |
| $P∧\text{c}$ | $\text{c}$ |
| $\text{c}∨¬P$ | $¬P$ |

questions.problem:
If $P$ is a statement, $\text{t}$ is a tautology, and $\text{c}$ is a contradiction, complete the following table of logical equivalences.

| Statement | Is Logically Equivalent To |
| --- | --- |
| $\text{t}∧\text{c}$ | {{field-1}} |
| $\text{c}∨\text{c}$ | {{field-2}} |
| $\text{c}∧¬P$ | {{field-3}} |
| $P∨\text{c}$ | {{field-4}} |
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following properties of tautologies and contradictions:

$$
\begin{aligned}A∨\text{t}=\text{t}\, &  & A∧\text{t} & =A \\ A∨\text{c}=A\, &  & A∧\text{c} & =\text{c} \\ \text{t}∨\text{t}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{t}∧\text{t} & =\text{t} \\ \text{t}∨\text{c}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{t}∧\text{c} & =\text{c} \\ \text{c}∨\text{t}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{c}∧\text{t} & =\text{c} \\ \text{c}∨\text{c}=\text{c}\, &  & \text{c}∧\text{c} & =\text{c}\end{aligned}
$$

The completed table is shown below.

| Statement | Is Logically Equivalent To |
| --- | --- |
| $\text{t}∧\text{c}$ | $\text{c}$ |
| $\text{c}∨\text{c}$ | $\text{c}$ |
| $\text{c}∧¬P$ | $\text{c}$ |
| $P∨\text{c}$ | $P$ |

questions.problem: Simplify the expression $(A∧B)∨(A∧¬B).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's simplify the expression using the properties of logical operations:

- First,  we use the distributive law (conjunction over disjunction):

$$
(A∧B)∨(A∧¬B)≡A∧(B∨¬B)
$$

- Next,  we use the fact that the disjunction of an expression and its negation is a tautology:

$$
A∧(B∨¬B)≡A∧\text{t}
$$

- Finally, we use the fact that the conjunction of an expression and a tautology gives the initial expression:

$$
A∧\text{t}≡A
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
(A∧B)∨(A∧¬B)≡A.
$$

- Next, we simplify the double negation:

$$

$$
(¬A∨B)∧(¬A∨A)≡(¬A∨B)∧\text{t}

$$
(¬A∨B)∧\text{t}≡¬A∨B
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
¬(A∧¬(B∧A))≡¬A∨B.

Example: 
                    Identifying Tautologies
canonical_examples.problem:
Complete the truth table below and use it to determine whether $(A \land B) \Rightarrow (B \Rightarrow A)$ is a tautology.

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\, A \land B \,$ | $\, B \Rightarrow A \,$ | $\, (A\land B) \Rightarrow (B \Rightarrow A) \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |  |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |  |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |  |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |  |
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
An expression is a tautology if it is always true, regardless of the inputs.

By completing the final column in the truth table below, we obtain the following:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\, A \land B \,$ | $\, B \Rightarrow A \,$ | $\, (A\land B) \Rightarrow (B \Rightarrow A) \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |

According to the table, $(A \land B) \Rightarrow (B \Rightarrow A)$ is always true. Therefore, it is a tautology.

| --- | --- | --- | --- |

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Applying Properties of Tautologies and Contradictions
canonical_examples.problem:
If $P$ is a statement, $\textbf t$ is a tautology, and $\textbf c$ is a contradiction, complete the following table of logical equivalences.

| Statement | Is Logically Equivalent To |
| --- | --- |
| $\textbf t \land \textbf c$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\phantom{\color{blue}P}}$ |
| $\textbf t \lor \textbf c$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\phantom{\color{blue}P}}$ |
| $P \land \textbf c$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\phantom{\color{blue}P}}$ |
| $P \lor \textbf c$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\phantom{\color{blue}P}}$ |
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall the following properties of tautologies and contradictions:

$$
\begin{aligned}A∨\text{t}=\text{t}\, &  & A∧\text{t} & =A \\ A∨\text{c}=A\, &  & A∧\text{c} & =\text{c} \\ \text{t}∨\text{t}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{t}∧\text{t} & =\text{t} \\ \text{t}∨\text{c}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{t}∧\text{c} & =\text{c} \\ \text{c}∨\text{t}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{c}∧\text{t} & =\text{c} \\ \text{c}∨\text{c}=\text{c}\, &  & \text{c}∧\text{c} & =\text{c}\end{aligned}
$$

The completed table is shown below.

| Statement | Is Logically Equivalent To |
| --- | --- |
| $\textbf t \land \textbf  c$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textbf c}$ |
| $\textbf t \lor \textbf  c$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textbf t}$ |
| $P \land \textbf c$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textbf c}$ |
| $P \lor \textbf c$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}P}$ |

Example: 
                    Simplifying Expressions Involving Tautologies and Contradictions
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's simplify the expression using the properties of logical operation

- First, we use that $X \Rightarrow Y  \equiv \neg X \lor Y {:}$

$$
(A \land \neg B)\Rightarrow \neg B \equiv
	\neg (A \land \neg B) \lor \neg B
$$

- Next, we use a De Morgan's law:

$$
{\color{blue}\neg (A \land \neg B)} \lor \neg B \equiv
	{\color{blue}(\neg A \lor \neg  \neg B)} \lor \neg B
$$

- Then,  we simplify the double negation:

$$
(\neg A \lor {\color{blue}\neg \neg} B) \lor \neg B  \equiv
	(\neg A \lor B) \lor \neg B
$$

- Next, we use the associative law:

$$
(\neg A \lor B) \lor \neg B  \equiv 
	\neg A \lor (B \lor \neg B)
$$

- Then,  we use the fact that the disjunction of an expression and its negation is a tautology:

$$
\neg A \lor  {\color{blue} (B \lor \neg B)}   \equiv
	\neg A \lor {\color{blue} \textrm{t}}
$$

- Finally, we use the fact that the disjunction of an expression and a tautology gives  a tautology:

$$
\neg A \lor  \textrm{t}  \equiv   \textrm{t}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
(A \land \neg B) \Rightarrow \neg B  \equiv   \textrm{t}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
An expression is a **tautology** if it is always true, regardless of the truth values of inputs. 

For example, let's consider the expression $A \lor \neg A,$ and fill out the corresponding truth table:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,\lnot A\,$ | $\,A \lor \neg A\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |

According to the table, $A \lor \neg A$ is always true. Therefore, it is a tautology.

Tautologies are represented by the symbol $\textbf t,$ so we write

$$
A \lor \neg A = \textbf t.
$$

tutorials.name: Properties of Tautologies and Contradictions
tutorials.problem:
Tautologies have the following properties:

- The disjunction of an expression and a tautology gives a tautology:

$$
A \lor \textbf{t} = \textbf{t}
$$

- The conjunction of an expression and a tautology gives the initial expression:

$$
A \land \textbf{t} = A
$$

Contradictions have the following properties:

- The disjunction of an expression and a contradiction gives the initial expression:

$$
A \lor \textbf{c} = A
$$

- The conjunction of an expression and a contradiction gives a contradiction:

$$
A \land \textbf{c} = \textbf{c}
$$

To prove these properties, we need to fill out the corresponding truth tables. For example, the truth table for the first property is shown below.

| $\,A\,$ | $\textbf{t}$ | $A \lor \textbf{t}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |

According to the table, $A \lor \textbf{t}$ is always true. Therefore, it is a tautology.

Finally, note the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{t}∨\text{t}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{t}∧\text{t} & =\text{t} \\ \text{t}∨\text{c}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{t}∧\text{c} & =\text{c} \\ \text{c}∨\text{t}=\text{t}\, &  & \text{c}∧\text{t} & =\text{c} \\ \text{c}∨\text{c}=\text{c}\, &  & \text{c}∧\text{c} & =\text{c}\end{aligned}
$$

Again, all of these properties can be proved using truth tables.
